A programming language by Ian Zepp · MIT

Meaning lives in the core,
not in the syntax.

Faber programs are stored as a semantic core, not as text in one particular language. Everything else — the words a human reads, the machine code that finally runs — is a rendering of that core. Change the rendering and the program does not change.

That single property is why Faber can print itself in Thai, and why the same function can come out as Rust, as LLVM IR, or as a GPU compute shader. It is one architectural bet, pointed in two directions.

Proof 1

One program, seven human renderings

These are not translations of a comment or a tutorial. They are the same program, and the compiler accepts every one of them. The keywords are supplied by a reader-locale pack; identifiers stay in canonical Latin so code stays portable between people who do not share a language.

f salve-munde.fab
English · la · read the docs in English →
functio salve(textus nomen) → textus {
    fixum textus msg ← "Salve, §!"(nomen)
    redde msg
}

incipit {
    fixum textus m ← salve("munde")
    nota m
}

Proof 2

One program, seven machine renderings

Same idea, other direction. This function — 

functio saturate(numerus x) → numerus {
    si x < 0 ergo redde 0
    si x > 255 ergo redde 255
    redde x
}

incipit {
    fixum numerus v ← saturate(300)
    nota v
}

— lowers to each of the following. Nothing here is hand-written or illustrative; every panel is literal radix emit output. The GPU panels come from an @ nucleum kernel: 

@ nucleum
functio scala(fractus<f32> x) → fractus<f32> {
    redde x + 1.0
}

LLVM IR is emitted from MIR directly — Faber reaches native code without passing through Rust, C, or any other source language.

f main.fab → target
radix emit --target rust main.fab — primary backend — reviewable source, then a native binary
// Generated by radix - do not edit
// Requires the faber language-runtime crate (add to Cargo.toml):
//   faber = { path = "../faber" }  # adjust path for your layout

fn saturate(x: i64) -> i64 {
    if x < 0 {
        return 0;
    };
    if x > 255 {
        return 255;
    };
    return x;
}

fn main() {
    let v: i64 = saturate(300);
    println!("{}", v);
}

radix emit --target llvm-text main.fab — MIR-backed — native code with no source language in between
; Generated by radix MIR LLVM IR probe - experimental artifact.
%FaberRtSliceV1 = type { ptr, i64 }
%FaberRtExitV1 = type { i32, i32 }
%FaberRtPtrResultV1 = type { i32, ptr }
%FaberRtStatusV1 = type { i32 }
@__faber_rt_v1_context = internal global ptr null
@__faber_rt_v1_status = internal global i32 0
declare void @__faber_rt_v1_fatal(ptr, %FaberRtSliceV1) noreturn

; @runtime __faber_rt_v1_diagnostic_nota_i64 category=host-integration
declare i32 @__faber_rt_v1_diagnostic_nota_i64(ptr, i64)

define i64 @saturate(i64 %l0) {
    entry:
      %l0.addr = alloca i64
      %t0.addr = alloca i1
      %t1.addr = alloca i64
      %t2.addr = alloca i1
      %t3.addr = alloca i64
      store i64 %l0, ptr %l0.addr
      br label %b0
    b0:
      %load0 = load i64, ptr %l0.addr
      %v0 = icmp slt i64 %load0, 0
      store i1 %v0, ptr %t0.addr
      %load1 = load i1, ptr %t0.addr
      br i1 %load1, label %b1, label %b2
    b1:
      store i64 0, ptr %t1.addr
      %load2 = load i64, ptr %t1.addr
      ret i64 %load2
    b2:
      %load3 = load i64, ptr %l0.addr
      %v2 = icmp sgt i64 %load3, 255
      store i1 %v2, ptr %t2.addr
      %load4 = load i1, ptr %t2.addr
      br i1 %load4, label %b3, label %b4
    b3:
      store i64 255, ptr %t3.addr
      %load5 = load i64, ptr %t3.addr
      ret i64 %load5
    b4:
      %load6 = load i64, ptr %l0.addr
      ret i64 %load6
}

define void @incipit() {
    entry:
      %l0.addr = alloca i64
      %t0.addr = alloca i64
      br label %b0
    b0:
      %call0 = call i64 @saturate(i64 300)
      store i64 %call0, ptr %t0.addr
      %load1 = load i64, ptr %t0.addr
      store i64 %load1, ptr %l0.addr
      %load2 = load i64, ptr %l0.addr
      %faber.context3 = load ptr, ptr @__faber_rt_v1_context
      %faber.diag.status3 = call i32 @__faber_rt_v1_diagnostic_nota_i64(ptr %faber.context3, i64 %load2)
      %faber.old.status3 = load i32, ptr @__faber_rt_v1_status
      %faber.has.error3 = icmp ne i32 %faber.old.status3, 0
      %faber.latched.status3 = select i1 %faber.has.error3, i32 %faber.old.status3, i32 %faber.diag.status3
      store i32 %faber.latched.status3, ptr @__faber_rt_v1_status
      ret void
}

define %FaberRtExitV1 @__faber_program_entry_v1(ptr %context) {
    entry:
      store ptr %context, ptr @__faber_rt_v1_context
      call void @incipit()
      %faber.entry.status = load i32, ptr @__faber_rt_v1_status
      %faber.entry.exit = insertvalue %FaberRtExitV1 { i32 0, i32 0 }, i32 %faber.entry.status, 1
      ret %FaberRtExitV1 %faber.entry.exit
}

    (func $saturate (export "saturate") (param $l0 i64) (result i64)

                      (local.set $t0 (i64.lt_s (local.get $l0) (i64.const 0)))

              (if (i32.eq (local.get $p0) (i32.const 1))
                  (then
                      (local.set $t1 (i64.const 0))
                      (return (local.get $t1))

              )

                      ;; v2 = (i64.gt_s (local.get $l0) (i64.const 255))
                      (local.set $t2 (i64.gt_s (local.get $l0) (i64.const 255)))
                      (if (local.get $t2)

                              (local.set $p0 (i32.const 3))

    (func $incipit (export "incipit")
          (local $l0 i64)
          (local $t0 i64)
          (local.set $t0 (call $saturate (i64.const 300)))
          (local.set $l0 (local.get $t0))

radix emit --target wgsl-text kernel.fab — GPU compute shader — from an @ nucleum kernel
// Generated by radix wgsl-text (supported-with-limitations compute source).

@group(0) @binding(0) var<storage, read> x_in: array<f32>;
@group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read_write> output: array<f32>;

@compute @workgroup_size(1, 1, 1)
fn scala(@builtin(global_invocation_id) id: vec3<u32>) {
  let i: u32 = id.x;
  if (i >= 1u) {
    return;
  }
  let x: f32 = x_in[i];
  output[i] = (x + 1.0);
}
radix emit --target metal-text kernel.fab — GPU compute shader — from an @ nucleum kernel
// Generated by radix metal-text (supported-with-limitations compute source).
#include <metal_stdlib>
using namespace metal;

kernel void scala(
    device const float* x_in [[buffer(0)]],
    device float* output [[buffer(1)]],
    uint id [[thread_position_in_grid]]
) {
  if (id >= 1) {
    return;
  }
    float x = x_in[id];
    output[id] = (x + 1.0f);
}
Proof 3

And it runs

Triga is a graphics and geometry engine written in Faber. These frames were produced by Faber source compiled to WGSL and executed on a GPU — no JavaScript, no three.js, no engine underneath doing the real work.

Fast enough to use like a script

Faber also runs without a build step. faber run --interpret takes source through parse, typecheck and MIR lowering, then steps the MIR in-process — no rustc, no linker, no build directory.

Same program, end to end, median of 15 runs (M-series Mac)
CommandWall clock
faber run --interpret (incl. full typecheck)4.4 ms
python3 script.py (no typecheck)13.3 ms

Reproduce with the scripting docs. A statically typed language should not be slower to start than a dynamic one, and it isn't.
